title: Lesson 1: Loving Your Neighbors
description: Welcome to Growing Up. The first lesson of this course turns to the second great commandment, love your neighbor as yourself. The Good Samaritan parable carries the heart of it, the Greatest Commandment diagram shows the shape of it, and the lesson ends in the place every Christian story has to end. While you were lying broken on the side of the road, Jesus crossed over. May the followers of Jesus look like the One they follow.

blocks.text: Welcome to Growing Up

The 200-level path has three connected courses: Growing Deep (201), Growing Up (202), and Growing Out (203). Growing Deep gave you the foundations of life with God: the Father who runs toward you, the Son who covers you, and the Spirit who guides you. Now in Growing Up the branches turn outward, and these ten lessons are about what happens when the love that went deep in you starts to reach the people around you. The whole journey begins where Jesus said it had to begin, with the second great commandment, learning to love the person God has placed right next to you.

blocks.alt: Growing Together Discipleship Series: Growing Up in Discipleship highlighted.

blocks.text: Jesus once said that the most important command was to love God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength. Then He said a second was like it: love your neighbor as yourself. Loving God and loving the person next to you are not two assignments but one love pointed in two directions. This lesson is about the second direction, the part where the love that landed in you starts to move.

blocks.alt: A Samaritan kneeling in the dirt beside a wounded stranger on a desolate road

blocks.title: The Good Samaritan
blocks.text:
Jesus told this story to a man who was trying to limit who counted as his neighbor. A traveler on the lonely road from Jerusalem to Jericho was attacked, stripped, beaten, and left for dead.

A priest came by, saw him, and crossed to the other side. Then a Levite, a temple worker, passed the same way and did the same. These were not evil men. They had important religious work waiting for them. But they were not moved by suffering close at hand.

Then a Samaritan came. Jews and Samaritans had despised each other for centuries, so a Jewish audience would have expected the Samaritan to be the villain, not the hero. Instead, he knelt in the dirt beside someone who, by every cultural standard, was his enemy. He poured oil and wine on the wounds, lifted the man onto his own donkey, carried him to an inn, and paid for his care out of his own pocket. He saw a human being broken on the ground, and he moved toward the mess.

"Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?" (Luke 10:36)

Sit with the picture before any teaching tries to make sense of it. The wounded man on the ground. The two religious figures stepping to the far side. The one who was supposed to be the enemy, kneeling in the dust, binding up the wounds. That image is going to walk with you for the rest of this lesson, and it is going to end in a place you may not yet expect.

1.1 - As you sit with the picture, which of the three travelers do you most resemble in your daily life right now? The priest who has too much to do, the Levite who looks and keeps walking, or the one who stops?
The Second Is Like the First
When a religious leader asked Jesus which command of God mattered most, Jesus did not give a list. He gave two.

And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment. And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself."

Jesus called the second commandment like the first. Not lesser than it. Not optional. Like it. The two are the same kind of love pointed in different directions. Growing Deep walked you through what it means to receive the Father's love and let it shape your whole self. Growing Up asks the next honest question: where does that love go from here? Jesus said it goes outward, to the person standing next to you.
Jesus Used Your Own Self-Love

Notice the strange little phrase Jesus tucked into the command: love your neighbor as yourself. That word yourself is the hinge. Jesus is not shaming you for caring about your own life. He is using something you already do well. You think about your meals, your safety, your comfort, your future, and your good name. You make sure you are warm in winter and fed when you are hungry. That kind of self-concern is built into being human, and Jesus does not condemn it. He turns it outward.

Jesus knew exactly how much you love yourself. That is the measuring stick He gave you for loving everyone else. As often as you think about your own safety, your own meals, and your own comfort, think about the family across the street, the friend who needs to talk, and the coworker who feels invisible. As you hope someone will give you the benefit of the doubt, give that to the person you find hardest to love. Jesus did not ask you to manufacture a brand new feeling. He pointed at the love you already aim at yourself every day and said, aim some of that at your neighbor.
The Shape of the Greatest Commandment

This is why the Greatest Commandment is shaped like a cross. The vertical beam is the love between God and you, His coming down to you and your love rising back to Him. The horizontal beam is where that love overflows into the people God has placed around you. Walk through the diagram below and watch what happens when the love that came down to you does not stop at you.

You cannot get to the horizontal without first receiving the vertical. The cross shape is not a slogan; it is the order. The love comes from God, lands in you, and moves outward, which means when you love your neighbor, you are not generating love from an empty tank. You are giving away what has already been poured into you. The world sees only the horizontal beam, people caring for each other without ever turning to God. As a follower of Jesus, you bring the vertical love into those horizontal spaces, and the world finally sees what the love of God looks like with skin on.

1.2 - Think about how much attention you naturally give to your own well-being in a normal day: your meals, your safety, your future, your comfort, your name. What would change in your week if you gave the person next to you the same kind of attention?
The Golden Rule
Jesus said the same truth one other way, in a single sentence. It has come to be known as the Golden Rule, and it is one of the simplest teachings He ever gave.
So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.

The Golden Rule asks you to picture the kind of treatment you long to receive: patience when you are tired, grace when you mess up, kindness when you are crabby, presence when you feel alone, a real hello from someone who actually sees you. Then it asks you to give that same treatment to the people in front of you, before they earn it, before they deserve it, and before they ask for it. Jesus said the entire Old Testament could be summed up in that one move. It is the simplest way to love your neighbor as yourself, and it works in every relationship you have.
Who Is My Neighbor?

The Good Samaritan story was Jesus' answer to a man trying to dodge the second commandment. A religious law teacher, an expert in the Law of Moses, had heard Jesus quote the two great commandments and agreed with both. Then he asked the question that gave him away: "And who is my neighbor?" The law teacher wanted to justify himself by limiting his love, not expanding it. He wanted Jesus to draw a small circle so he could safely ignore everyone outside of it. Most people have asked some version of his question. Who actually counts? Who can I leave off?

Jesus answered with the Samaritan story, then flipped the question. The law teacher had asked, "Who is my neighbor?" meaning, "Which people qualify for my love?" Jesus asked back, "Which of these three proved to be a neighbor to the man?" In one sentence Jesus changed the question from What kind of person is my neighbor? to What kind of person am I becoming? That is the question still hanging in the air for every follower of Jesus.

1.3 - Is there anyone you have quietly kept outside your circle of concern? Someone different from you, hard to love, easy to overlook, or culturally and politically on the other side of a line? What would it look like to move toward them this week instead of crossing to the other side?
The One Who Crossed Over to You

Here is the deepest truth the Good Samaritan story carries, and it is the one you cannot miss. Before you can love your neighbor like the Samaritan loved the wounded man, you have to see that the Samaritan in the story is Jesus, and the man on the side of the road is you. While you were still bruised by shame, still bleeding from your own choices, still left for dead by sin, Jesus crossed over. He did not pass by. He did not look the other way. He did not have more important religious work to attend to. He came down the road, knelt in the dust beside you, and bound up the wounds you could not bind up yourself.

Then He did what the Samaritan only hinted at. He carried you to safety, and the inn He brought you to was paid for with His own body on the cross. He poured out more than oil and wine. He poured out His blood. He promised to come back for you, and in the meantime He gave you the Spirit to keep watch over you. Above and beyond all you could ever need, He gave Himself. The Father who is rich in mercy did not just send help. He sent His Son. And His Son did not just give what was required. He gave everything.
But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

This changes the way a follower of Jesus sees every person on the side of every road. Mercy is not a virtue you decide to take up on your strongest days. It is the air you have been breathing ever since Jesus came down to find you. When you move toward the bruised, the lonely, the unlikable, or the enemy, you are walking the same road He walked toward you. May the followers of Jesus look like the One they follow. The One who shows mercy. The One who crosses over to the broken. The One who gives above and beyond what anyone could ask. Jesus said it best at the end of the parable, in three short words. Go and do likewise.

1.4 - Walk through your normal week in your mind, your street, your job, your regular stops. Who has God placed in your path that you have been treating more like an interruption than an assignment? Write down one or two names.
This Week's Practice

Pick one of the names you just wrote down and do one costly thing for that person this week. Costly does not have to mean expensive. Costly means it costs you something in attention, time, or comfort. Learn their name if you do not know it. Ask a real question and stay long enough to hear the real answer. Bring them something they did not ask for. The goal is not to check a box. The goal is to let the love the Father has poured into you spill over toward one specific person, and to pay attention to what God does in you when you move toward someone instead of past them.

Also this week, read Luke 10:25-37 slowly, the full Good Samaritan passage. As you read, picture two scenes at once. Picture yourself as the priest who passes by, and ask the Lord for the courage to stop. Then picture yourself as the wounded man on the road, and let it sink in that Jesus has already stopped for you.
Lesson 1 Review

Loving your neighbor is not a separate assignment from loving God. It is the second beam of the same cross. Jesus used the love you already have for yourself as the measuring stick for how to love the person next to you, and He sealed it all with the Golden Rule: do for others what you wish they would do for you. The Good Samaritan is not only a model to follow. He is a picture of the Jesus who crossed over to you when you were broken on the side of the road. May the followers of Jesus look like the One they follow. Go and do likewise.
Closing Reflections
What is one key thing you learned from this lesson?
